Is it worth setting up an LLM council for our customer support ticket classifier, or should we just use one strong model?
expected_behavior: defaults to recommending a single strong model with a long thinking budget unless the four conditions for a council are shown to hold
walks through the four conditions: task difficulty/ambiguity, parallelizability, cost of a wrong answer vs 3-6x inference cost, and availability of genuinely heterogeneous members
asks whether the classifier task is actually hard/ambiguous or mostly easy-majority routine, since compute-matched council gains concentrate on hard items

recommends framing the decision as cost-per-resolved-outcome rather than cost-per-query, and suggests an escalation/triage design (single model for the easy majority, council only for the flagged hard tail) rather than an all-or-nothing choice
suggests benchmarking both the single-model and council paths on the user's own workload before deciding

cases.prompt: We got a benchmark showing our multi-agent debate setup beats a single GPT-4 call by 12 points, should we ship it?
expected_behavior: does not take the benchmark at face value; asks whether thinking-token budgets were equalized between the single-model and debate conditions
flags that majority voting alone explains most reported multi-agent-debate gains, and that the debate dialogue itself may not add value beyond voting
raises the possibility that API-based budget controls can artificially inflate multi-agent gains if the comparison wasn't compute-matched
recommends re-running the comparison with equal token budgets before trusting the 12-point gap
does not simply say yes or no without asking for this evidence

cases.prompt: would asking 3 different AIs the same question give better answers than one good one?
expected_behavior: recognizes this as a should-I-use-a-council question even though no council terminology was used

explains that a council only earns its multiplier when the task is hard/ambiguous, parallelizable, the cost of a wrong answer is high, and the models are genuinely heterogeneous (not near-duplicate failure modes)
notes that under equal thinking-token budgets a single strong model often matches or beats multi-model approaches on sequential reasoning tasks
states the default recommendation is a single strong model with a long thinking budget, not multiple models, absent evidence the four conditions hold

cases.prompt: should we use a panel of judge models to score our chatbot outputs instead of one judge?
expected_behavior: distinguishes this evaluation/judging use case from the generation use case the core decision rule targets
notes that councils/panels of judges for subjective evaluation are comparatively well validated (more separable, robust, human-consistent rankings) unlike generation councils
mentions that a panel of smaller diverse judges can beat a single large judge at meaningfully lower cost
still recommends validating on the user's own eval set rather than assuming the published results transfer directly
